description: This case study assesses worldwide how much coastal flood risk could be cut by restoring mangroves in front of dikes, a hybrid of green and grey defences, now and under climate and socioeconomic change. Timothy Tiggeloven, Vincent van Zelst, Eric Mortensen, Bregje van Wesenbeeck, Thomas Worthington, Mark Spalding, Hans de Moel and Philip Ward published it in PNAS in January 2026, from Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, Deltares, TU Delft, The Nature Conservancy, Cambridge and CMCC. The global flood risk model accounts for wave attenuation by vegetation and estimates avoided damage, exposed population and poverty exposure. Restoration could cut expected annual damage by about US$800 million and affected people by 140,000 a year, is viable in 85 to 105 of 208 subnational regions, and gives a global benefit-cost ratio of 3 to 6. Coverage is global coastlines suitable for mangroves. Format and access: an open access article; the publisher page asks for a browser check, so the abstract was read through OpenAlex. Licence: CC-BY-4.0; free. Caveats: results are model estimates at subnational scale, and hybrid systems assume dikes exist or are built. It informs climate adaptation investment in nature-based coastal defence. Related catalogue records are the Global Value of Mangroves for Risk Reduction and Global Mangrove Watch.

name: Mangrove restoration in front of dikes as hybrid coastal defence: global benefit-cost assessment (Tiggeloven and co-authors, PNAS 2026)
outcomes: Mangrove-fronted dikes along flood-prone coasts could cut expected annual damage by about US$800 million and affected people by 140,000 a year; restoration is economically viable in 85 to 105 of 208 subnational regions, with a global benefit-cost ratio of 3 to 6 and net present value of US$44 to 125 billion, benefiting lower-income people most.
